citeinfo.title: International Manganese Samples—The Donnel Foster Hewett Collection

descript.abstract:
International manganese samples in this collection were acquired from various countries, typically by geoscientists and university professors of the corresponding region. Manganese samples from the United States were collected in the field primarily by other USGS scientists noted in the dataset. The dataset corresponds to Hewett's physical collection of manganese-bearing samples re-established in 2023-2024 under the National Geological and Geophysical Data Preservation Program. Individual samples were assigned a new USGS Sample ID once the sample locality was identified. Each new sample number has an assigned cabinet letter and drawer number so that users can readily locate physical samples in the reorganized collection. The dataset includes location (state and site-specific names such as mines, claim(s), prospects, and deposit groups), latitude and longitude, origin of coordinates, sample type, collector of sample (if given), mineral name (if given), qualitative volume estimates for manganese oxide in each sample, and mass of samples in kilograms and grams. It is important to note that one mine, claim, or prospect can have multiple samples with different USGS identification numbers.
This collection of manganese samples was assembled by Donnel Foster Hewett (1881-1971), an economic geologist and mineralogist with the USGS for fifty-nine years, serving for a period of time as Chief of the USGS's Metalliferous Geology Section. His study of manganese deposits aided in wartime steel production and earned him the nickname, "Mr. Manganese.” He is credited with the discovery of two major economic deposits, including the Minas Ragra mine, a major vanadium producer in the Pasco Region of Peru. Throughout the first half of the 20th century, Hewett provided an overall deeper understanding of metalliferous ore genesis in various geological settings.
descript.purpose: This dataset is part of the 2023-2024 USGS Critical Mineral Commodity Specialist Collections Preservation effort for public and scientific use under the National Geological and Geophysical Data Preservation Program (NGGDPP). The dataset is also available through an on-line repository named ReSciColl (Registry of Scientific Collections). Retrospective studies on manganese oxide ore deposits, manganese characteristics from various mineral systems, and other geochemical, mineralogical, or spectroscopic studies are deemed as appropriate use of this collection.

attracc.attraccr: A RMSE (root mean square error) compared geospatial locations given by the collector against georeferenced images of deposits given in a corresponding scientific paper. All deposit coordinates tested in RMSE was calculated in Arcgis Pro® using WGS84 datum. The location accuracy or RMSE value for these coordinates is 0.2 meters. Earth Point© coordinates were verified for accuracy in ArcGIS Pro® by testing ten centroids of a described PLSS (Public Land Survey System) location given by the sample collector. Results found that the average horizontal distance between Earth Point© and ArcGIS® coordinates is less than five kilometers. If a sample had a PLSS location, Earth Point© was then used to calculate centroid coordinates for that location. The LasBela Mining District is a unique instance where a coordinate centroid was generated from known deposits identified in "Colombo Plan, 1960, Reconnaissance geology of part of west Pakistan: The Government of Canada." This literature was sent to Hewett personally upon his request for sample locations. Deposits in this literature matched USGS MRDS (Mineral Resources Data System) KML files, where a centroid for LasBela District was generated.

dataqual.logic: All locations given for individual samples were reported by the collector. If the sample location given by the collector could not be verified with PLSS, USGS MRDS or other reference materials, they were not used in this collection.
dataqual.complete: This dataset represents manganese-rich samples collected throughout Donnel F. Hewett's career. There are over 700 physical mineral samples from around the world. These samples are from diverse metalliferous ore deposits including lacustrine, carbonate-replacement (CRD), LCT pegmatite, and volcanogenic massive sulfide (VMS). Essential information is provided about individual samples: mass in grams and kilograms; mineral type (if noted by collector); sample type (reference hand sample(s),powder, sand, and/or pebble); and, an estimated percentage of manganese oxides for each sample. Approximately ninety percent of this collection was geo-chemically analyzed by Hewett through 1911-1951

procstep.procdesc: Samples were recovered from labeled boxes on pallets and one dresser. In many instances, samples were stored in labeled boxes, rock bags, glass jars, glass vials and/or paper containers. These labels matched locations in Hewett's journal or the collectors field note. Collector field notes were stored with the corresponding sample. Information about state location, additional area descriptions, mineral name (if given by collector), collector name, deposit name and/or mine name were generated from these sources. Initially, all samples were searched using USGS MRDS on-line database.

If an individual sample could not be matched to a MRDS file or no PLSS was provided by the collector, a government mineral database or a corresponding scientific journal (typically authored by the collector) was used in an effort to find coordinates.

Sample locations were identified and coordinates were transformed to the WGS84 datum. Some coordinates could be found in a corresponding scientific journal and were transformed in NCAT (NGS Coordinate Conversion and Transformation Tool). Images of deposit locations found in scientific journals were georeferenced in ArcGIS Pro®. Deposits that had a PLSS description were transformed in Earth Point©. Samples with known locations had collector name, mineral name (if provided by collector), mine name and, additional descriptions entered into the dataset.

The volumetric abundance in percent of manganese oxide minerals present was visually estimated for each unique sample. Manganese oxide volume estimates were based on the presence of black to dark steel-grey minerals with a submetallic to resinous luster and botryoidal, massive, or fibrous habit. Some manganese oxides appeared velvety, silky, or sooty with more massive forms best described as earthy. If manganese oxide volume percent was over fifty, a Y or Yes was assigned to that sample. While a sample can have a twenty percent manganese oxide volume estimate, it is important to note that the same sample might contain another non-oxide manganese mineral (for example, rhodochrosite, knebelite, and bementite).

Information about individual sample mass was recorded into our dataset under the "Mass_kilograms" and "Mass_grams" headings. Each USGS Sample ID has a mass recorded into the dataset. It is important to note that some samples are contained in more than one box but has one USGS Sample ID assigned to it. The mass of multiple boxes assigned to one USGS Sample ID are summed.

D.F. Hewett sample identification numbers were assigned to a new, USGS Sample ID. Hewett sample identification numbers and the associated USGS sample numbers are under the "Hewett_Sample_ID" and "USGS_Sample_ID" headings in our dataset, respectively. USGS Sample ID's are labeled on sample boxes, directly on large hand samples or on sample jars.

Labeled samples are stored in rock cabinets. The Rock cabinets are labeled with a cabinet letter and a drawer number for ease of sample retrieval, e.g., USGS Sample ID MC0042 from Harshaw Mining District, Arizona is stored in A3; cabinet letter A, drawer 3. Our dataset denotes this information under the "Drawer_Number" and "Cabinet_Letter" headings.

attr.attrdef: Manganese mineral identification. Minerals were identified by D.F. Hewett or another scientist who personally collected the sample.

edom.edomvd: A mineral name was not given for these samples.

attrdomv.udom: Of the forty-three minerals named in our dataset by collectors, fourteen out of forty-three are manganese oxide minerals. Most minerals in this collection are associated with manganese. Historical mineral names that are not approved by IMA (International Mineralogy Association) as of 2024, were not used in our dataset.

attr.attrdef: Additional descriptions aid in identifying sample locations such as historic mine names, mine owner names, mining districts, and native reservations. Additional descriptions may include specific geologic formations, e.g., Chinle Formation in Nevada, groups, e.g., Owl Group in New Mexico, occurrences, e.g., Fort Payne Chert in Tennessee, and mountain ranges from where the sample originated. Rarely, a specific mine adit, stope, tunnel, or drift name was given in association with a particular sample.

edom.edomvd: The collector did not provide additional descriptions for these samples.

Additional descriptions aid in identifying sample locations such as historic mine names, mine owner names, mining districts, and native reservations.

attr.attrdef: Original source of WGS84 coordinates.

edom.edomvd: Coordinates calculated in ArcGIS Pro® were done so using deposit maps. Geo-referencing was completed in WGS84 datum. A centroid was calculated in ArcGIS Pro® using the same datum, for the Las Belas Mining District, Pakistan. A RMSE (root mean square error) test was applied to all ArcGIS® coordinates to check location accuracy.
Earth Point© automatically calculated the centroid coordinates of a PLSS given by the sample collector in WGS84 datum.

NCAT was applied in instances where written coordinates of deposits were available in government mineral databases or scientific literature. An NCAT transformation was performed on these coordinates to ensure use in WGS84 datum.
A mineral record data system (MRDS) is a USGS deposit database that provides coordinate location in WGS84 datum.
